core.h: Theme map: which poems fit which question
core.p: Questions usually name a theme (e.g. ‘the effects of conflict’, ‘power’, ‘anger’, ‘identity’, ‘nature’, ‘loss’). Find the theme, then pick a partner.

bullets: **Exposure + Charge of the Light Brigade**: soldiers’ deaths; futility vs glory; soldier-poet vs Poet Laureate.
**Exposure + Poppies**: war and home; the closed door vs the open door.
**Exposure + The Prelude**: nature’s power; killer vs teacher.
**Charge + The Man He Killed**: obedience; not reasoning why vs failing to find a reason.
**Charge + Belfast Confetti**: Balaclava and Raglan in both; glory vs its legacy.
**A Poison Tree + Cousin Kate**: hidden vs voiced anger; both end in revenge.
**Half-Caste + No Problem**: racism, Caribbean voices, humour as a weapon.
**The Class Game + Cousin Kate**: class judgement; defiance vs ruin.
**What Were They Like? + War Photographer**: civilians seen from a distance; memory vs images.

callouts.p: Pairing a pre-1900 poem with a modern one gives you easy, rich AO3 contrast (e.g. Tennyson 1854 vs Weir 2009).
Do not pick your favourite poem regardless of the question. A weaker poem that fits the theme beats a brilliant one that does not.

core.h: Ten best pairings (with the hinge idea)
core.p: A great pairing has one clear similarity and one clear difference. The ‘hinge’ is the sentence that opens your essay.

core.h: Pre-1900 and modern (useful for AO3 contrasts)

model: Power: Sennacherib (non-human power destroys an army)
Loss: Poppies (loss from the home front)
Identity: The Man He Killed (soldier identity, enemy as mirror)
Nature: The Prelude (nature as teacher vs killer)
exam.q: Quick drill: for each theme (power, loss, identity, nature, family), name the best partner for Exposure and say your hinge in one sentence.
exam.tip: Do this drill for every poem the week before the exam.

mistakes.r: Pick the partner that best fits the theme, then build every paragraph around it.
mistakes.w: Choosing a second poem with no real link to the question’s theme.

mistakes.r: Compare in every paragraph; the top band rewards ‘perceptive comparisons’ throughout.
mistakes.w: Writing about the two poems separately.

mistakes.r: Use the theme map: decide in one minute.

summary: In Section B you are given one named Conflict poem and must choose a second to compare; this note maps every poem to its themes and gives the strongest pairings, so you can choose a partner in under a minute in the exam.
